title: FY2026 Education request combines K–12 grants while raising IDEA and charter funding
description_short: FY2026 Education request combines K–12 grants while raising IDEA and charter funding
description_medium: The Education Department’s FY2026 request proposed a $2 billion K–12 Simplified Funding Program, while also requesting $14.9 billion for IDEA Grants to States—$677.5 million above FY2025—and $500 million for charter-school grants, up from $440 million in 2024. The proposal therefore did not increase only charter funding. The exact aggregate K–12 cut depends on which programs and baselines are counted.
description_long: The Education Department’s fiscal year 2026 budget request proposed consolidating several elementary and secondary education programs into a new $2 billion K–12 Simplified Funding Program and eliminating or consolidating other programs in the relevant account. The detailed budget tables do not support the original statement that charter schools were the only line item proposed for an increase. They request $14.9 billion for IDEA Grants to States, $677.5 million above the FY2025 level, and $500 million for charter-school grants, compared with $440 million in 2024. Those amounts were requests to Congress, not enacted appropriations. The sources describe separate program lines and do not by themselves establish the final funding schools received or the consequences for particular districts. A reported aggregate reduction of roughly $4.5 billion may use a broader K–12 comparison than the cited account tables; the precise baseline and programs included need to be made explicit before retaining that total. The supported event is the administration’s FY2026 proposal to restructure K–12 grants while requesting increases for both IDEA and charter grants.

frozen_original_snapshot.synopsis: Education Secretary Linda McMahon's proposed FY2026 budget included a $4.5 billion cut from K-12 spending — a 15% reduction. The budget maintained spending for Title I and IDEA (disabilities) while consolidating or eliminating other programs. Charter school funding was the only line item recommended for an increase. McMahon told lawmakers cuts were realized by "eliminating duplicative or ineffective programs" and giving states "more flexibility." Republicans praised the shift toward "more educational options" — code for school privatization through vouchers and charter expansion.

title: Brookings says Witkoff made eight Moscow trips without visiting Kyiv as confidence in U.S. mediation fell
description_short: Brookings says Witkoff made eight Moscow trips without visiting Kyiv as confidence in U.S. mediation fell
description_medium: In an April 29, 2026 Brookings commentary, Steven Pifer wrote that U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff had traveled to Moscow eight times since March 2025 without visiting Kyiv. Pifer cited polls showing 70% of Ukrainians did not expect U.S.-brokered talks to succeed and 28% viewed the United States as reliable. The claim that the diplomacy was one-sided is Pifer’s assessment.
description_long: In an April 29, 2026 Brookings commentary, former U.S. ambassador Steven Pifer wrote that Steve Witkoff, the Trump administration’s chief Russia–Ukraine negotiator, had traveled to Moscow eight times since March 2025 but had not visited Kyiv. Pifer argued that the pattern made U.S. mediation appear one-sided and contributed to declining Ukrainian confidence. He cited polling in which 70 percent of Ukrainians did not expect U.S.-brokered talks to succeed and a separate poll in which 28 percent considered the United States a reliable partner. These are claims and interpretations reported in Pifer’s policy commentary; the Brookings page does not itself provide the underlying itinerary records or full poll methodology. The figures do not establish that Witkoff’s travel caused the reported attitudes. The original entry’s March 2025 date marks the start of the travel-count period, while the sourced commentary and snapshot of the claim are from April 2026. The corrected account therefore attributes the travel count, polling, and bias assessment to Pifer and dates the reporting to the commentary.
notes: The supplied event date is the April 29, 2026 commentary; the input date_start of March 1, 2025 appears to mark the start of Witkoff’s Moscow-trip period and may need metadata correction.

title: Trump’s 2025 disclosure reports nearly $800 million tied to World Liberty Financial
description_short: Trump’s 2025 disclosure reports nearly $800 million tied to World Liberty Financial
description_medium: Reuters’ review of Trump’s 2025 financial disclosure reported more than $1.4 billion in total crypto-related income, including nearly $800 million tied to World Liberty Financial and $635 million from separate Trump meme-coin sales. Reuters attributed more than $520 million of the WLF amount to token sales and more than $250 million to sale of business interests. The full $1.4 billion was not WLF income.
description_long: A June 30, 2026 Reuters report reviewed President Donald Trump’s annual financial disclosure for 2025 and reported more than $1.4 billion in income from crypto-related ventures. Reuters attributed nearly $800 million to World Liberty Financial, the crypto venture co-founded by Trump and his sons. That reported WLF amount included more than $520 million from token sales and more than $250 million from sale of interests in the business. Reuters separately reported $635 million from Trump meme-coin sales. The two streams should not be combined under the WLF label: the disclosure and Reuters account distinguish the company’s reported income from the separate coin business. Reuters also notes that WLF income was split among family members. These are reported disclosure figures, not an independent audit of net profit, cash received by Trump personally, or company-wide revenue. The disclosure supports a narrower account of the scale and composition of the reported 2025 crypto income, but it does not by itself prove that any government policy caused or improperly benefited the ventures.
notes: Correction applied: separates nearly $800 million tied to World Liberty Financial from roughly $635 million in separate meme-coin income.

title: Trump’s 77% trade-deficit claim compared selected monthly figures, not the full-year result
description_short: Trump’s 77% trade-deficit claim compared selected monthly figures, not the full-year result
description_medium: FactCheck.org reported that Trump’s January 27, 2026 claim of a 77% trade-deficit reduction appears to compare January 2025’s $128.8 billion monthly deficit with October’s $29.2 billion figure. The White House did not confirm that calculation. Using full-year data, FactCheck.org said the 2025 goods-and-services deficit was 0.2% below 2024. The original November 2025 date predates the sourced claim.
description_long: On January 27, 2026, President Donald Trump said he had cut the U.S. trade deficit by 77 percent. FactCheck.org examined the figure and said it appeared to compare the monthly goods-and-services deficit in January 2025, $128.8 billion, with October’s $29.2 billion deficit. The White House did not confirm that this was the calculation. FactCheck.org cautioned that comparing two selected months does not establish the annual trend. After full-year data were released, its February 19 analysis reported that the 2025 goods-and-services deficit was about $901.5 billion, 0.2 percent below 2024. The first account also reported a 3.9 percent decline for February through November compared with the same period in 2024; that is a different interval and should not be mixed with the later full-year comparison. The corrected entry should be dated to the January 2026 statement and February 2026 analyses, not November 2025. These sources support describing the 77 percent figure as a selective monthly comparison, not the full-year change, and do not establish every trade-policy or import-causation claim in the original.
notes: Reason: The supplied correction says the stored November 2025 event date predates Trump’s January 2026 claim and the February 2026 fact-checks.
Proposed correction: Set the event date to 2026-02-03 for the first fact-check, or split/retime if the later February 24 full-year comparison is the intended event.

frozen_original_snapshot.title: Trump Lied: Tariffs Did NOT Slash Trade Deficit by 77%
frozen_original_snapshot.synopsis: Throughout 2025 and into 2026, Trump made sweeping false claims about tariffs eliminating the U.S. trade deficit. In a January 2026 Iowa speech, he claimed: In one year I've slashed our gaping trade deficit by a staggering 77%. At the World Economic Forum, he repeated the claim. In February 2026, he posted in all caps: THE UNITED STATES TRADE DEFICIT HAS BEEN REDUCED BY 78% BECAUSE OF THE TARIFFS. The Commerce Department's actual data told the opposite story: the overall 2025 trade deficit fell only 0.2% from 2024. Worse, the U.S. merchandise goods deficit — the exact measure Trump's tariffs were meant to fix — hit a record $1.24 trillion in 2025, up 2% from 2024. Economists explained that Trump was cherry-picking a single anomalously low monthly figure (October 2025) against the artificially inflated January 2025 figure, when importers had stockpiled goods ahead of tariffs. FactCheck.org found that through the full 10 months Trump was president in 2025, the cumulative deficit was actually 4.1% higher than the same period in 2024. PolitiFact rated his deficit-reduction claims False. The merchandise trade deficit set a new record precisely because U.S. companies imported massive quantities of semiconductors and tech equipment to build out AI infrastructure.

proposed_correction: Date the claim to January 27, 2026 and state that FactCheck.org found it appears to compare January and October monthly deficits; full-year 2025 deficit fell 0.2% from 2024.
unsupported_original_claims: That the 77% statement was made in November 2025.
The claim that tariffs caused the full-year goods deficit to reach a record or explain semiconductor imports; these cited analyses do not establish those assertions.
The assertion that FactCheck.org found the ten-month deficit was 4.1% higher; its February 3 analysis reports different interval figures, and its February 19 full-year figure is −0.2%.

exact_gap: The White House did not confirm the arithmetic behind the 77% claim; do not characterize the comparison as definitively Trump’s method.

title: MAGA Inc. invitation listed a $1 million price for a Mar-a-Lago dinner featuring Trump
description_short: MAGA Inc. invitation listed a $1 million price for a Mar-a-Lago dinner featuring Trump
description_medium: WIRED reviewed an invitation for MAGA Inc.’s March 1, 2025 candlelight dinner at Mar-a-Lago featuring President Trump; it stated “$1,000,000 per person” to reserve a seat. Axios independently reported the price and said the super PAC charged as much as $1 million for Trump-featured fundraisers. The sources do not establish that every invited guest paid or that a named donor made a particular pitch.
description_long: A March 1, 2025 candlelight dinner at Mar-a-Lago featured President Donald Trump and was promoted by MAGA Inc., a pro-Trump super PAC. WIRED reported that an invitation it obtained asked prospective attendees to pay $1 million per person to reserve a seat. Axios independently verified the invitation detail and reported that MAGA Inc. was charging as much as $1 million per plate for fundraisers featuring Trump. The documents establish an advertised price for a seat and the event’s connection to the super PAC; they do not show that every invitee attended or paid the listed amount. The supplied reporting does not substantiate the original entry’s separate claim that crypto entrepreneur Ari Schiermeyer donated $1 million and used the dinner to pitch Trump on a token project. Nor does the seat price alone establish an illegal exchange or a particular policy benefit. The supported event is the high-priced fundraising invitation, dated to March 2025. Any account of individual payments, access conversations, or a specific policy pitch requires separate reporting or financial records.

title: Appeals court upheld a preliminary block on Trump’s White House ballroom project
description_short: Appeals court upheld a preliminary block on Trump’s White House ballroom project
description_medium: On August 7, 2026, the D.C. Circuit upheld a preliminary injunction stopping construction of the administration’s $400 million White House ballroom project, finding that congressional authorization was lacking. Reuters reported that the court stayed its order for 14 days to allow an appeal. This was not a final merits ruling. The supplied sources do not substantiate the Oracle data-center allegation.
description_long: On August 7, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld a preliminary injunction halting construction of a proposed $400 million ballroom at the White House, on the site of the demolished East Wing. Reuters reported that the court found the administration had begun the project without congressional authorization. The panel’s order was stayed for 14 days to allow the administration to seek Supreme Court review, so the decision should be described as an appellate ruling on preliminary relief rather than a final judgment permanently barring the project. The original record’s February 2025 date does not match this court event. The cited Reuters and AP coverage supports the project cost, the injunction, and the authorization issue. It does not support the separate claim that Oracle was involved in a data-center footprint under an expanded White House campus, nor the broader characterization of the project as a personal real-estate scheme. Those allegations require distinct sources. The narrow entry documents the court’s intervention and its procedural posture.

title: Inspector general found Lafayette Park was cleared for fence installation, not Trump’s church visit
description_short: Inspector general found Lafayette Park was cleared for fence installation, not Trump’s church visit
description_medium: A 2021 Interior Department inspector general review found that Park Police cleared Lafayette Park on June 1, 2020, to allow contractors to install anti-scale fencing. The report said evidence did not support the claim that the clearing was ordered to enable President Trump’s walk to St. John’s Church. Trump walked through the park at 7:01 p.m., after the 6:23–6:50 p.m. operation.
description_long: The Department of the Interior Office of Inspector General reviewed the U.S. Park Police operation at Lafayette Park on June 1, 2020. Its report said the evidence did not support a finding that the park was cleared to allow President Donald Trump to survey damage or walk to St. John’s Church. Instead, the review found that the operation was planned to let a contractor safely install anti-scale fencing, following property destruction and officer injuries during protests on May 30 and 31. The clearing began at 6:23 p.m. and ended at 6:50 p.m.; Trump walked from the White House through Lafayette Park to the church at 7:01 p.m. The report also noted that not everyone could hear all dispersal warnings. This does not erase criticism of the force used or resolve every question about individual officers’ actions, but it directly contradicts the original description’s assertion that the clearing was ordered for a staged photo opportunity. The narrower account should center the official review’s findings and retain the sequence of events without stating a motive the investigation did not substantiate.
